title: Chapter 134 — The Chase—Second Day
paragraphs: At daybreak, the three mastheads were promptly manned again.
"Do you see him?" cried Ahab, after allowing a little time for the light to spread.
"See nothing, sir."
"Turn up all hands and make sail! He travels faster than I thought — the topgallant sails! — aye, they should have been kept on her all night. But no matter — he's only resting for the rush."

Let it be said here that this persistent pursuit of one particular whale, kept up through day into night and through night into day, is by no means unheard of in the South Sea fishery. For such is the wonderful skill, the foresight born of experience, and the unshakable confidence acquired by some great natural geniuses among the Nantucket captains, that from simply observing a whale when last sighted they will, under certain given circumstances, predict pretty accurately both the direction in which he will keep swimming for a while out of sight, and his probable rate of progress during that time. In these cases the whale-fisherman does somewhat as a pilot does when he is about to lose sight of a coast whose general trend he knows well, and which he wants to return to shortly, but at some further point: just as this pilot stands by his compass and takes the exact bearing of the cape now in view, so as to be surer of hitting the remote, unseen headland he will eventually reach, so the fisherman stands at his compass with the whale; for after the creature has been chased and carefully marked through several hours of daylight, then, when night hides the fish, its future wake through the darkness is almost as settled in the hunter's shrewd mind as the pilot's coast is in his. So, to this hunter's wondrous skill, a wake — that proverbially fleeting thing written in water — is for all desired purposes nearly as reliable as the steadfast land. And just as the mighty iron Leviathan of the modern railway is so familiarly known in its every pace that men, watches in hand, time his rate as doctors time a baby's pulse, and say casually that the up train or the down train will reach such and such a spot at such and such an hour, so, almost, there are occasions when these Nantucketers time that other Leviathan of the deep by the observed humor of his speed, and say to themselves that so many hours from now this whale will have gone two hundred miles, and will have about reached this or that degree of latitude or longitude. But for this sharpness to succeed at all in the end, the wind and the sea must be the whaleman's allies; for what use at the moment to the becalmed or windbound sailor is the skill that assures him he is exactly ninety-three leagues and a quarter from his port? Many further subtle points concerning the chase of whales can be inferred from these statements.
The ship tore on, leaving a furrow in the sea like the one a stray cannonball makes when it turns plowshare and furrows up the level field.

"By salt and hemp!" cried Stubb, "but this swift motion of the deck creeps up one's legs and tingles at the heart. This ship and I are two brave fellows! — Ha, ha! Someone pick me up and launch me spine-first on the sea — for, by live-oaks! my spine's a keel. Ha, ha! We go the gait that leaves no dust behind!"
"There she blows — she blows! — she blows! — right ahead!" was now the cry from the masthead.

"Aye, aye!" cried Stubb. "I knew it — you can't escape — blow on and split your spout, O whale! The mad fiend himself is after you! Blow your trumpet — blister your lungs! — Ahab will dam off your blood, as a miller shuts his watergate on the stream!"

And Stubb was only speaking for nearly the whole crew. The frenzies of the chase had by now worked them up into a bubbling ferment, like old wine fermenting anew. Whatever pale fears and forebodings some of them might have felt before, these were now not only kept out of sight by their growing awe of Ahab, but broken up and routed on all sides, like timid prairie hares scattering before the bounding bison. The hand of Fate had snatched all their souls; and by the stirring dangers of the day before, the torment of the past night's suspense, and the fixed, unfearing, blind, reckless way their wild ship went plunging toward its flying target — by all these things their hearts were bowled along. The wind that swelled their sails into great bellies and rushed the vessel on with arms as invisible as they were irresistible seemed the symbol of that unseen power which so enslaved them to the race.

They were one man, not thirty. For just as the one ship that held them all, though it was put together from all sorts of contrasting things — oak, and maple, and pine; iron, and pitch, and hemp — yet had all these running into one another in the single solid hull, which shot on its way both balanced and steered by the long central keel, so all the individualities of the crew — this man's courage, that man's fear, guilt and guiltiness — all these varieties were welded into oneness, and all were directed toward that fatal goal which Ahab, their one lord and keel, pointed to.

The rigging was alive. The mastheads, like the tops of tall palms, sprouted outspreading tufts of arms and legs. Clinging to a spar with one hand, some reached out the other with impatient waves; others, shading their eyes from the vivid sunlight, sat far out on the rocking yards; every spar bore its full crop of mortals, ready and ripe for their fate. Ah! how they still strove through that infinite blueness to seek out the thing that might destroy them!

"Why don't you sing out for him, if you see him?" cried Ahab, when some minutes had passed since the first cry and no more had been heard. "Sway me up, men; you have been deceived. Moby Dick does not cast one odd jet that way and then disappear."

It was just so; in their headlong eagerness the men had mistaken something else for the whale's spout, as the event itself soon proved; for hardly had Ahab reached his perch, hardly was the rope made fast to its pin on deck, when he struck the keynote for an orchestra that made the air vibrate as if with the combined discharge of rifles. The triumphant shout of thirty buckskin lungs was heard as — much nearer the ship than the place of the imaginary jet, less than a mile ahead — Moby Dick burst bodily into view! For the White Whale now revealed his nearness not by any calm and lazy spouting, not by the peaceful gush of that mystic fountain in his head, but by the far more wondrous phenomenon of breaching. Rising at his utmost speed from the farthest depths, the Sperm Whale in this way booms his entire bulk into the pure element of air, and, piling up a mountain of dazzling foam, shows where he is to a distance of seven miles and more. At such moments the torn, enraged waves he shakes off seem to be his mane; in some cases this breaching is his act of defiance.

"There she breaches! There she breaches!" was the cry, as in his immeasurable bravado the White Whale tossed himself salmon-like to Heaven. Seen so suddenly in the blue plain of the sea, and set off against the still bluer edge of the sky, the spray he raised glittered and glared unbearably for the moment, like a glacier; and it stood there, gradually fading and fading from its first sparkling intensity to the dim mistiness of a shower advancing up a valley.
"Aye, breach your last to the sun, Moby Dick!" cried Ahab. "Your hour and your harpoon are at hand! — Down! Down, all of you, but one man at the fore. The boats! — stand by!"

Ignoring the tedious rope-ladders of the shrouds, the men slid to the deck like shooting stars by the lone backstays and halyards, while Ahab, less dartingly but still rapidly, was lowered from his perch.
"Lower away," he cried, as soon as he had reached his boat — a spare one, rigged the afternoon before. "Mr. Starbuck, the ship is yours — keep away from the boats, but keep near them. Lower, all!"

As if to strike quick terror into them — being by this time the first to attack — Moby Dick had turned and was now coming for the three crews. Ahab's boat was in the center; and cheering his men on, he told them he would take the whale head-and-head — that is, pull straight up to his forehead — which is not an uncommon thing; for within a certain distance such a course keeps the coming attack out of the whale's sideways vision. But before that close range was reached, and while all three boats were still as plain to his eye as the ship's three masts, the White Whale, churning himself into a furious speed, rushed among the boats almost in an instant, as it were, with open jaws and lashing tail, and offered appalling battle on every side; and heedless of the irons darted at him from every boat, he seemed intent only on annihilating each separate plank those boats were made of. But skillfully maneuvered, wheeling ceaselessly like trained war-horses on the field, the boats evaded him for a while, though at times only by a plank's breadth; while all the time Ahab's unearthly war cry tore every other cry but his to shreds.

But at last, in his untraceable twists and turns, the White Whale so crossed and recrossed, and in a thousand ways so tangled the slack of the three lines now fast to him, that they shortened and, of themselves, hauled the doomed boats toward the irons planted in him; though now for a moment the whale drew a little aside, as if to rally for a more tremendous charge. Seizing that chance, Ahab first paid out more line, and then began rapidly hauling and jerking it in again — hoping that way to clear it of some snarls — when look! — a sight more savage than the embattled teeth of sharks!

Caught and twisted — corkscrewed in the tangles of the line — loose harpoons and lances, with all their bristling barbs and points, came flashing and dripping up to the chocks in the bow of Ahab's boat. Only one thing could be done. Seizing the boat-knife, he reached with precise care within — through — and then out beyond — the rays of steel; dragged in the line beyond them, passed it inboard to the bowsman, and then, cutting the rope twice near the chocks, dropped the intercepted bundle of steel into the sea, and was all fast again. At that instant the White Whale made a sudden rush among the remaining tangles of the other lines; by doing so he irresistibly dragged the more entangled boats of Stubb and Flask toward his flukes, dashed them together like two husks rolling on a surf-beaten beach, and then, diving down into the sea, disappeared in a boiling maelstrom, in which, for a while, the fragrant cedar chips of the wrecks danced round and round like grated nutmeg in a swiftly stirred bowl of punch.

While the two crews were still circling in the water, reaching out after the revolving line-tubs, oars, and other floating gear; while little Flask, slanting, bobbed up and down like an empty vial, twitching his legs upward to escape the dreaded jaws of sharks; and Stubb was lustily singing out for someone to ladle him up; and while the old man's line — now parting — allowed him to pull into the creamy pool to rescue whom he could — in that wild simultaneous rush of a thousand massed perils, Ahab's still unstruck boat seemed drawn up toward Heaven by invisible wires, as, arrow-like, shooting straight up out of the sea, the White Whale dashed his broad forehead against its bottom and sent it turning over and over into the air, until it fell again, gunwale downward, and Ahab and his men struggled out from under it like seals from a seaside cave.

The whale's first upward momentum — changing its direction as he struck the surface — carried him along it, without his willing it, to a little distance from the center of the destruction he had made; and with his back to it he now lay for a moment, slowly feeling from side to side with his flukes; and whenever a stray oar, a bit of plank, or the least chip or crumb of the boats touched his skin, his tail swiftly drew back and came sideways, smiting the sea. But soon, as if satisfied that his work for that time was done, he pushed his pleated forehead through the ocean and, trailing the intertangled lines after him, continued on his way to leeward at a traveler's steady pace.

As before, the watchful ship had seen the whole fight and again came bearing down to the rescue; lowering a boat, she picked up the floating sailors, tubs, oars, and whatever else could be caught hold of, and landed them safely on her decks. Some sprained shoulders, wrists, and ankles; livid bruises; wrenched harpoons and lances; hopeless tangles of rope; shattered oars and planks — all these were there; but no fatal or even serious harm seemed to have come to anyone. As with Fedallah the day before, Ahab was now found grimly clinging to his boat's broken half, which made a comparatively easy float; nor did this mishap exhaust him as much as the previous day's had.

But when he was helped onto the deck, all eyes were fixed on him; for instead of standing by himself he still hung half his weight on the shoulder of Starbuck, who had so far been the first to help him. His ivory leg had been snapped off, leaving only one short, sharp splinter.
"Aye, aye, Starbuck, it's sweet to lean sometimes, whoever the leaner may be; and I wish old Ahab had leaned more often than he has."
"The ferrule has not held, sir," said the carpenter, now coming up; "I put good work into that leg."
"But no bones broken, sir, I hope," said Stubb with true concern.

"Aye! And all splintered to pieces, Stubb! — do you see it? — But even with a broken bone, old Ahab is untouched; and I count no living bone of mine one jot more me than this dead one that's lost. Neither white whale, nor man, nor fiend can so much as graze old Ahab in his own proper and inaccessible being. Can any lead touch that floor down there, any mast scrape that roof up there? — Aloft there! Which way?"
"Dead to leeward, sir."
"Up helm, then; pile on the sail again, shipkeepers! Down with the rest of the spare boats and rig them — Mr. Starbuck, away, and muster the boats' crews."
"Let me first help you toward the bulwarks, sir."
"Oh, oh, oh! How this splinter gores me now! Cursed fate! That the unconquerable captain in the soul should have such a cowardly mate!"
"Sir?"

"My body, man, not you. Give me something for a cane — there, that shattered lance will do. Muster the men. Surely I have not seen him yet. By heaven, it cannot be! — missing? — quick! Call them all."
The old man's half-spoken thought was true. When the company was mustered, the Parsee was not there.
"The Parsee!" cried Stubb — "he must have been caught in — "
"May the black vomit wrench you! — run, all of you, above, below, cabin, forecastle — find him — not gone — not gone!"
But they quickly came back to him with the news that the Parsee was nowhere to be found.
"Aye, sir," said Stubb — "caught among the tangles of your line — I thought I saw him dragging under."

"My line! My line? Gone? — gone? What does that little word mean? — What death-knell rings in it, that old Ahab shakes as if he were the belfry? The harpoon, too! — toss over the litter there — do you see it? — the forged iron, men, the white whale's — no, no, no — blistered fool! this hand did dart it! — it's in the fish! — Aloft there! Keep him nailed — quick! — all hands to the rigging of the boats — collect the oars — harpooners! the irons, the irons! — hoist the royals higher — a pull on all the sheets! — helm there! Steady, steady for your life! I'll girdle the unmeasured globe ten times; yes, and dive straight through it, but I'll slay him yet!"

"Great God! Show yourself, if only for one single instant," cried Starbuck; "never, never will you capture him, old man — in Jesus' name, no more of this; it's worse than devil's madness. Two days chased; twice stove to splinters; your very leg snatched from under you once more; your evil shadow gone — all good angels mobbing you with warnings — what more do you want? — Shall we keep chasing this murderous fish till he swamps the last man? Shall we be dragged by him to the bottom of the sea? Shall we be towed by him to the infernal world? Oh, oh — it is impiety and blasphemy to hunt him any more!"

"Starbuck, lately I've felt strangely moved toward you, ever since that hour when we both saw — you know what — in one another's eyes. But in this matter of the whale, let the front of your face be to me as the palm of this hand — a lipless, featureless blank. Ahab is forever Ahab, man. This whole act is immutably decreed. You and I rehearsed it a billion years before this ocean rolled. Fool! I am the Fates' lieutenant; I act under orders. See to it, underling, that you obey mine. — Stand round me, men. You see an old man cut down to the stump, leaning on a shattered lance, propped up on a lonely foot. That is Ahab — his body's part; but Ahab's soul's a centipede that moves on a hundred legs. I feel strained, half stranded, like ropes that tow dismasted frigates in a gale; and I may look so. But before I break, you'll hear me crack; and till you hear that — know that Ahab's hawser tows his purpose yet. Do you believe, men, in the things called omens? Then laugh aloud, and cry encore! For before they drown, drowning things will rise twice to the surface; then rise again, to sink forevermore. So with Moby Dick — two days he's floated — tomorrow will be the third. Aye, men, he'll rise once more — but only to spout his last! Do you feel brave, men, brave?"
"As fearless fire," cried Stubb.

"And as mechanical," muttered Ahab. Then, as the men went forward, he muttered on: "The things called omens! And yesterday I talked the same way to Starbuck there, about my broken boat. Oh! how valiantly I try to drive out of others' hearts what's clinched so fast in mine! — The Parsee — the Parsee! — gone, gone? And he was to go before — but still was to be seen again before I could perish — how's that? — There's a riddle now that might baffle all the lawyers, backed by the ghosts of the whole line of judges — it pecks my brain like a hawk's beak. I — I will solve it, though!"
When dusk came down, the whale was still in sight to leeward.

So once more the sail was shortened, and everything passed nearly as on the night before; except that the sound of hammers and the hum of the grindstone were heard until nearly daylight, as the men toiled by lantern light at the complete and careful rigging of the spare boats and the sharpening of their fresh weapons for the next day. Meanwhile, out of the broken keel of Ahab's wrecked boat the carpenter made him another leg; while, still as on the night before, Ahab stood slouched and fixed within his scuttle, his hidden, heliotrope glance — sun-seeking, like the flower — turned back ahead of time on its dial, set due east for the earliest sun.
